en: The Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui compiled this second [section], which further summarizes the characteristics of the seven great assemblies. The designation "great" (mahā) is based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

according to the doctrinal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Hīnayāna, it is taught that all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are accomplished through the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are further divided...
Regarding the internal and external:

this is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; yet it is quiescent but not perfected, as it is still distinguished by the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—being coarse and shallow.

This is the Buddha-Tathāgata’s speech according to the intentions of others for the sake of worldly convention; it possesses a name but lacks reality. Although it is called "great," the meaning of "great" is not established therein. This is not how it is described in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

This means that it is all-pervasive and inclusive; its essence is nowhere absent and there is nothing that is not it. It is not designated as "great" in dependence upon something small, but rather receives this name by virtue of its own essential nature; therefore, it is called "Great."

Now, as for why the seven meanings taught in this sutra are all called "great," it is because within these seven meanings all phenomena are subsumed—namely, emptiness and existence, faculties and objects, matter and mind, and essence and appearance. In every particle of dust and every phenomenon, there is nothing that is not universally pervasive and nothing that is not inclusively contained. This serves to shatter provisional views and cause one to know the true meaning, as the text below states: "These are uniformly named the Seven Greats; their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, being the Tathāgata-garbha. Yet the world lacks knowledge and is deludedly attached to them as having the nature of causes and conditions or of spontaneity. These are all merely the conceptual calculations of the discriminating consciousness; they consist only of verbal expressions and entirely lack real meaning."

This means that the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are identical with the nature (dharmatā), and since both the nature and the characteristics are all-pervasive, they alone may be called the supreme, ultimate Great [Vehicle]; how could this be the same as the provisional teachings which speak of "self-characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa)?
The text has three parts;
first, the presentation of the objection.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has often spoken of the principle of the harmony of causes and conditions, saying that all the various transformations in the world arise through the manifestation of the harmony of the four great elements.”
Thus he recounted what he had heard in the past:
"How is it that the Tathāgata rejects both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity? I do not now understand to which category this meaning belongs."
I now speak this difficult [teaching].
To "push aside" means to cast out and reject.
"Please, out of compassion and pity, reveal to sentient beings the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation."
This is a request for instruction.
Through skillful means, [the Buddha] establishes that there are four great causal conditions which harmoniously combine to produce all transformations.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena are unborn; now they are likewise unceasing. Birth, cessation, coming, and going are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
Now, because one uses conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to doubt the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this objection arises.
Second, the permission to explain has three parts:
first, pointing to the intent and indicating the topic.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Previously, you grew weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi; therefore, I shall now reveal the Ultimate Truth for you."

"The combination of causes and conditions and the manifestation of the four great elements are all teachings of the Hīnayāna; that all phenomena are unborn and are solely the Tathāgatagarbha is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Second, reiterating the doubt and citing 'A'."
"Why do you further entangle yourself with worldly frivolous discourse and the causes and conditions of false conceptualization?

Although you are widely learned, you are like a man who knows how to describe medicines but cannot distinguish them when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly pitiable."
"Enveloped" refers to doubt.
Since the Buddhas know all secrets without exception, it is said that they "prescribe medicine.
Now, hearing that all dharmas are the Tathāgatagarbha is called the manifestation of the true medicine before one.
Raising past expedient means to cast doubt upon the present reality is called "inability to discern.
Third, the command to listen attentively:
"Listen now with earnest attention; I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so as to enable those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future to penetrate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s holy command.
He was instructed to grant permission for the proclamation, so that both the present and the future might be benefited.
Second, the actual exposition, in two parts:
1. A general refutation based on reasoning: "Ānanda!
As you have said, it is through the combination of the four great elements that the various transformations of the world are manifested."
Ānanda! If the essential nature of those great elements were not a state of combination, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not combine with various forms.

If they were to combine, they would be identical to a magical illusion: beginning and end mutually forming one another, birth and cessation continuing in succession; death following birth, and birth following death, like a whirling firebrand that never rests.
"Ānanda! Just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to become water.
The first four lines cite what is being conceptualized; the subsequent six lines briefly refute that it is not a composite.

If the intrinsic nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) were not inherently harmonious, then these elements would not be in harmony, just as space and material form differ in their resistance and non-resistance.

If one refutes "harmony" by asserting that harmony is dissolved, then if the essential nature of the great elements were itself a composite, it would constitute arising and ceasing; thus, from beginning to end, there would be only arising and ceasing.

This explains the characteristics of birth and death. The first phrase explains the establishment of the characteristic; the second phrase explains continuity—meaning that birth can establish death and so forth, and death can continue birth and so forth—which refers to the present birth continuing the past birth.
The two metaphors following the "spinning" [wheel] illustrate, respectively, continuity and mutual establishment,
as explained in the text. Second,
refuting by citing the specific nature [of the self], in seven parts:
I. The Nature of Earth (pṛthivī-dhātu).
Four parts: 1. Citing an example to indicate it:
"Observe the nature of earth: its coarse form is the great earth; its subtle form is minute dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the ultimate atom)."
"If one analyzes the characteristics of the ultimate limit of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) into seven parts, and further analyzes the *paramāṇu* [itself], it is simply the nature of emptiness.
A *paramāṇu* is a particle without spatial divisions; it is the ultimate limit of the characteristics of form.
An atom (*paramāṇu*) is a subtle particle that possesses spatial dimensions.

Now, this sutra refers to such a spatially extended particle as the "characteristic of the limit of form" (*rūpaparyantanimitta*); one need not attempt to reconcile this with other scriptural passages, as it is presented according to the specific context of this sutra.
2. Establishing the Principle through Extensive Refutation: "Ānanda!
If these atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form."
This establishes the principle based on the proposition.

Since one can analyze form (*rūpa*) to reveal emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one may likewise synthesize emptiness to manifest form; only then can it be said that they mutually establish and continue one another.
As for your current question:
"Because of their combination, the various manifested forms of the world arise.
This restates the doubt that is to be resolved; wishing to refute it, he first restates the position:
"Observe this single atom of dust: by the combination of how many spaces does it exist?"
"One should not hold that atoms combine to form an atom.
Below this, there is a detailed refutation based on reasoning: it is irrational for emptiness to combine to form matter.

Since you allow that matter is analyzed into emptiness, you must also allow that emptiness combines to form matter. Atoms are the ultimate minimum; how much emptiness would be required to constitute their functional utility?
If atoms were to combine, they would themselves possess spatial divisions and thus could no longer be considered atoms.
Furthermore, if one analyzes an atom until it dissolves into emptiness, by means of how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is empty space constituted?
"To say that the combination of material forms constitutes emptiness is to deviate from the true meaning.
Space is the greatest of things, while the atom (paramāṇu) is the smallest; when breaking the small to form the great, how many atoms are employed?
If material forms combine, then the combined forms are not empty."
If they were to merge with emptiness, that which merges with emptiness would not be form.
This shows that neither form nor emptiness establishes the other.
Form merges with form to produce form, and emptiness merges with emptiness to produce emptiness; because each follows its own kind, their merging does not involve mutual transformation.
"Form may still be analyzed, but how can emptiness be joined?
This is a repeated reprimand regarding the error in the meaning of joining with emptiness.
To analyze form in order to clarify emptiness is a method found in both the teachings and contemplative practice.
When emptiness combines to form form, there is nothing upon which to rely internally or externally.
As the preceding text states, "Just as empty space does not know of various forms," if one claims that they combine to form a continuous succession, all such assertions are false.
3. Harmonizing with Ultimate Reality:

"You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know, and manifests in accordance with their karma."
This clarifies true form (*rūpa*).
The first phrase points to fundamental delusion; the following three phrases beginning with "Tathāgata" reveal the essence of the Dharma.
The Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), within the single Dharma-realm mind.
The nature of form is true emptiness; this is the truth within the conventional. The nature of emptiness is true form;
this is the convention within the true. The repeated mention of "nature" reveals the truth and the conventional within the middle way.

This means that raising one immediately encompasses the three, and speaking of the three bodies is itself the one; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they separate, and are thus called the Secret Treasury—this is the true element of earth.

The latter two lines of the "Pure" section describe the measure of its virtuous qualities: it is "pure" because it is in accord with non-delusion and possesses untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas; it is called "primordial" (*mūla-prakṛti*) because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); and it is called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) because it is omnipresent.
This, then, is the complete fulfillment of lineage, essence, virtue, and magnitude.

If one understands this dharma and accomplishes the three sublime contemplations, one will finally know that a single mote of dust contains all Buddha-dharmas, all mind-dharmas, and all sentient-being dharmas; that there is nothing which does not reside within a single minute particle, wherein one immediately beholds Vairocana.
To see oneself is to see all phenomena;
as it is with a single atom, so it is with all phenomena—the following cases are all to be understood accordingly.

This passage reveals how [the Buddha] accords with conditions according to sentient beings: the ten realms of sentient beings differ in their outflows (*āsrava*) and non-outflows, their karmas are likewise different, and the material phenomena they induce vary in purity and impurity, and so forth.
4. Conclusion and Reprimand of Deluded Sentiment:

"The ignorant of the world are deluded into regarding things as having causes and conditions or being of spontaneous nature; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever."

All those outside the Buddhist fold and those of the Lesser Vehicle who rely on provisional teachings are termed "ignorant," for they do not understand the ultimate meaning; they are termed "deluded" because they fail to realize reality, and they are said to be "attached" because they cling to established names and forms.
This is a general refutation of all that is false and illusory.
The consciousness-mind is illusory; it arises from inversion, and through the accumulation of delusion upon delusion, what reality could there be?
Second, the nature of fire, in four parts:
First, the general indication of the absence of self-nature: "Ānanda!
The nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions."

The fire produced through dependent origination has no sovereign; that which lacks a sovereign is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), existing only as a false appearance through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Second, the extensive refutation by means of examples, in two parts:
first, citing an example to pose the inquiry.
“Observe those households within the city that have not yet eaten; when they wish to cook their food, they hold a *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal) in their hands and seek fire from the sun.
This is the illustration.
A *sūryakānta* is a fire-producing mirror.

“Ānanda! That which is called a ‘conjunction’ is like myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now constitute a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, when its basis is examined, each has their own body; all have their respective origins, ethnicities, and names—such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa of the Kāśyapa caste, and even Ānanda of the Gautama lineage.”
This is an illustration by citation.

By citing the multitude, it clarifies harmony and union; because the particular constitutes the general, and the general must necessarily contain the particular, he cites three individuals to manifest their distinctions.
"Gautama, this is called 'Earth-Supreme' (Kṣitigarbha), and it is also called 'Solar Lineage' (Sūryavaṃśa).
Uruvilvā means 'Wood-apple Grove' (Bilva-vana). Ānanda!"

If this nature of fire exists because of a combination of causes, then when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire emerge from within the mirror or does it emerge from the tinder?
"Is it from day to day?"—
the interrogation of this statement is thus understood.
Second, refutation by means of reasoning.
“Ānanda, if the sun were to come here, it would naturally burn the mugwort in your hand, and all the forests from which it comes would likewise be consumed by fire.
This refutes the theory that the sun is produced.
"From the sun to your hand it is forty thousand *yojanas*; why is it that wherever it shines, nothing else encounters heat, yet only the mugwort in your hand is burned?
If it emerges from within the mirror, being able to emerge from the mirror itself to burn the mugwort, why does the mirror not melt?"
"If you were to take it up in your hand, it would still not exhibit any signs of heat; how then could it melt?
This refers to the "shattered mirror" (po jing).
The first four lines constitute a direct refutation (*zheng po*), while the final three lines constitute a reductio ad absurdum (*zong po*).
Fire can overcome metal; upon encountering it, metal must melt and dissolve. Externally, fire can burn moxa, and internally, it can liquefy a mirror.
Now, since you are not so [affected], you should not have emerged from the mirror.
"If fire arises from the tinder, why must it depend on the sun, the mirror, and their mutual contact with light before the fire is produced?
This refutes the theory that fire arises from the tinder.
If the tinder were capable of producing fire, why would no fire emerge when the sun and mirror are not joined?
If fire must arise only after these elements come together, it is evident that it does not emerge from the moxa itself.
"Observe this closely again: the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the moxa grows from the earth; from what direction has the fire traveled to reach here?"
In summary, there is no source from which it arises.
Since it does not emerge from these three locations, from where could fire be produced?
One should know that it must not exist.
"The sun and the mirror are far apart; they neither blend nor combine. It is not reasonable that the fire-light should exist spontaneously without a source.
This refutes the notion of a causeless blending.
Since the sun and the mirror are not close, there is no sense of their blending.
Since fire does not exist within the conditions, it is impossible for there to be fire apart from those conditions; such a principle simply does not exist.
Third, the reconciliation with ultimate reality:
"You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm."
This clarifies the true fire.

The first phrase points to fundamental delusion; the three phrases beginning with "Tathāgata" manifest the essence of the Dharma; and the two phrases beginning with "pure" clarify its measure of brilliance—all are explained as previously stated.
"It follows the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they know.
Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place; if they hold it throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it will arise filling the whole world."
"Arising throughout the entire world, how could it have a specific location?
It manifests according to karma.
This clarifies that following conditions is also to be understood as previously explained.
4. Conclusion and Reprimand of Deluded Sentiment:

"The ignorant of the world are deluded into regarding things as having causes and conditions or as being of spontaneous nature; these are all merely conceptual calculations of the discerning mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and lack any real meaning whatsoever."
As can be understood from the text.
Third, the nature of water, in four parts:
first, a general statement of its lack of intrinsic nature.
“Ānanda! The nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.
Because the conditions of water are impermanent, it is said to be unfixed.”
To follow the movement of phenomena and then cease is the characteristic of non-fixity.
Second, the extensive refutation by citing specific instances, which has two parts:
first, citing instances to pose the inquiry.
"Just as the great illusionists of Śrāvastī, such as the sages Kapila, Cakraka, Padma, and Mahāsadā, seek the essence of the moon to mix with their magical elixirs."
When these masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon—
does this water emerge from within the gem,
or does it exist spontaneously in space?
"Does it come from the moon?
Kapila replied, "It is yellowish-red in color.
Cakraka replied, "It is a wheel."
*Padma* means "red lotus flower.
*Hāsata* is not clearly defined.
These are all followers of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
The essence of the Great Yin is the moon.
Fangzhu refers to a water-producing pearl.
When the Great Yin is at its zenith, one directs the pearl toward it to seek water.
The three locations—the moon, the jewel, and space—have been examined.
Second, the refutation through logical reasoning:
"Ānanda!..."

If it were derived from the moon, it would still be able to cause water to emerge from afar; all the trees and forests it passes should likewise discharge streams. If they do so, why wait for the water produced by the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror used to collect dew)?
"It does not flow; this clarifies that water does not descend from the moon.
This refutes the theory that the moon produces [water].
The first five phrases directly cite and refute [the opponent's view]: since the moon moves through the human realm at a distance equal to that of the sun, it is said to be "far away."
Wherever the moonlight shines, everything merges into a flowing stream; why then would it emerge solely from the pearl?

As for the "flowing" mentioned in the latter four lines, they form a dual conclusion that is incorrect: if everything where the light shines becomes a flow, what need is there for the pearl to emerge?
If it were without outflows, this would demonstrate that the nature of this water does not come from the moon.
If it emerged from the pearl, then water should constantly flow from within this pearl; why then must one wait for the middle of the night to receive it when the white moon is present?
"It would mean that water arises from the breaking of the pearl.
If the pearl were to produce water, then since it is always present, there would be a constant flow; why would it not produce water even without waiting for the reflection of the moon?

If it were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless; from humans to gods, all would be submerged together in a vast flood. How then could there still be those who travel by water, on land, or through the air?"
This refutes the arising from emptiness.
If emptiness were to produce water, then wherever there is emptiness, there would be water; who then would not be drowned?
Since emptiness is all-pervasive, water would likewise be omnipresent, and humans, devas, heaven, and land should no longer exist as distinct entities.
"Tao" means that water has submerged something.
"Observe this more closely: the moon ascends from the sky, the pearl is held in the hand, and the basin for receiving the pearl was set out by a person. From what direction does the water flow here?"
"In sum, there is no source from which it arises.
The moon rises from the heavens; the pearl is held within the hand; the basin is placed by a person; but from where does the water come?
The moon and the pearl are far apart; they neither blend nor combine. It cannot be that the essence of the moon exists spontaneously without a source."
This refutes the causeless nature of the breaking of harmony.
As for what is called "crystal," it is that which flows from the essence of the Great Yin (the moon).
Since it does not exist even within its conditions, how could it possibly exist apart from them?
3. Harmonizing with the True Principle:

"You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition."

If one holds a pearl in one place and water emerges in that same place, yet one were to hold it throughout the entire dharma-realm and cause it to arise filling the entire dharma-realm, such that its arising fills all worlds—how could there be any fixed location?
"Manifesting in accordance with karma"—
the commentary on this section is as before.
Fourth, the conclusion rebukes deluded sentiment.

"The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [conditions] as causes and conditions or as arising from spontaneity; all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning."
4. The nature of wind has four aspects:
first, a general indication of non-arising:
"Ānanda!..."
"The nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
The nature of wind has no form; it is manifested through movement and stillness.
Second, the extensive refutation by citing specific instances, in two parts:
1. Citing an event to indicate the point of inquiry:
"When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, if a corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and touches a person nearby, a slight breeze will then brush against that person's face."
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*,
arise from empty space,
or originate from that person's face?
The *saṃghāṭī* is the great robe (*mahācīvara*).
"Kāṣāya" means "dyed with a ruined color.
When the robe moves here and the wind brushes against there, neither the two locations nor the space between them arise; one should know that they are all illusory.
2. Refutation by Reasoning: "Ānanda!

If this wind were to emerge from the corner of my *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; the robe would flutter and fly away, separating from your body. Now, as I preach the Dharma in this assembly with my robe hanging down, look at my robe: where is the wind?"
"There should be no place within the robe where wind can be stored.
This refers to the arising [of wind] from a tattered robe.

Regarding the first five phrases, if the robe were separated from the body, it would be broken; the nature of wind is not still. If it were to arise within the robe, one should see it fluttering and moving; why is this not the case now?

The six subsequent lines below provide an analogy to refute [the claim that] there is no wind: the Buddha’s robe does not flutter even when it hangs down, yet how is it that your *kāṣāya* alone produces wind?
It is not necessarily the case that there is some hidden space within the robe that prevents it from moving.
"If wind were born from space, your robe would not move; for what reason is there no brushing?
This section below refutes the birth of wind from space.
This is the direct citation and refutation: if space were to give rise to wind, why would it require your movement of the robe for it to exist?
"If emptiness is eternally present, wind should always arise.
This and what follows constitute a successive series of challenges.

Now, these two lines challenge [the opponent] based on the constant presence of emptiness: since the nature of emptiness is without cessation, wind should likewise be ever-present; why then does no wind emerge when the cloth is not being moved?
"If there were no wind, space would perish.
This is difficult to refute regarding the perishing of space when there is no wind.
If space gives rise to wind, then when the wind does not arise, space should be non-existent.
"If the cessation of wind can be seen, what is the appearance of the cessation of space?
It is difficult to establish the cessation of space.
One should know that wind ceases when objects are motionless; but when space itself were to cease, by what means could it be demonstrated or established?
"If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called empty space.
This is the difficulty regarding arising and ceasing being non-empty:
empty space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and as such, it is without arising and ceasing.
That which now possesses arising and ceasing cannot be called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"It is named space; how then can wind emerge?
This is a rhetorical objection concluding that space does not give rise to wind.
The nature of wind is movement, while empty space is quiescent; how could that which is quiescent give rise to movement?

"If the wind were produced from the face itself that it brushes against, then it should brush you as it arises from that face. Since you yourself are straightening your robe, why does it instead brush against it?"
"His face is blown upon.
The first two phrases state the position; from "from that" onwards, the four phrases refute it.

If the face of the person being fanned were to produce wind, it should blow favorably [toward him]; you should receive the fanning, and you yourself should adjust your robes, for the wind does not emerge from you. How then could that wind blow back against his face?

"Examine this closely: your robe is adjusted upon you, your face belongs to that person, and empty space is tranquil and does not participate in movement; from which direction does the wind stir and come here?"
This is a further examination.
The face and space are distinct, and movement and stillness differ in essence; from where does the wind come to blow upon that face?
Since the nature of wind and space are separate, they neither blend nor combine; it cannot be that the wind arises spontaneously from nowhere within the mind.
This refutes the notion that there is no cause for the dissolution of harmony.
Since movement and stillness are not the same, they are said to be separated by nature (*prakṛti*).
Mind is itself nature; it is only because the phrasing has changed that it is expressed thus.
3. Harmonizing with the Ultimate Principle:

"You are utterly unaware that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition."
Ānanda! Just as when you alone slightly move your robe, a subtle breeze arises;
so too, when it sweeps through the entire Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and pervades the world, how could it have a specific location?
"Manifesting according to karma.
Fourth, the conclusion rebukes deluded sentiments:

"The ignorant of the world are confused regarding causes and conditions as well as the nature of spontaneity; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind. They consist only of verbal explanations and lack any real meaning whatsoever."
5. Emptiness (śūnyatā) has four aspects:
first, a general indication of the absence of intrinsic nature.
"Ānanda, emptiness is formless; it is manifested through form."
"Emptiness has no substance; the place where form is absent is what manifests as emptiness. Because it exists only in relation [to form], it lacks intrinsic nature.
Second, the extensive refutation by means of examples, which has two parts:
first, citing examples to pose the inquiry.

“It is like those in the city of Śrāvastī who live far from the river—Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Purohitas and Caṇḍālas—who have newly established their dwellings and dig wells in search of water.”
This cites the actual instances.
*Kṣatriya* means "Field-King.
*Brāhmaṇa* means "Pure-Vow."
*Viśya* means "sitting merchant.
*Śūdra* means "farmer.
*Purohita* [here rendered as *Pulastya*] means "sharp-witted," and also implies "swift."
Caṇḍāla means "killer.

When one foot of earth is excavated, there is one foot of empty space within it; likewise, when ten feet of earth are excavated, one obtains ten feet of empty space in between. The depth of the empty space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth removed.
Does this emptiness arise because of the earth?
Because of the digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
This is the formal introduction.
According to the amount of earth that is excavated, one perceives the depth of the space revealed.

Both emptiness and form are equally provisional; they exist in mutual dependence, and their essence is not separate from form. This present investigation is intended to make known their illusory nature.
2. Refutation by Reasoning:
"Ānanda! If this space were produced spontaneously without a cause, why was it not unobstructed before the earth had been excavated?"
"One sees only the great earth, with no passage through it at all.
This refutes the theory of causeless arising.
If space were causeless, why was there none when one first dug?
What exists after the excavation?
It cannot be established without a cause.

If it were produced from the earth, then at the time the earth is excavated, one should see space entering; if the earth is first excavated without space entering, how can empty space be said to be produced from the earth?
"Breaking the earth to produce [space]—this is precisely the refutation.

The first three phrases state the refutation: if space were produced from the earth, then when the earth is removed from a well, one should see empty space emerging from the earth and entering the well."
If the four lines regarding the earth below conclude that [space] is not [inherent], yet you see the earth emerge while not seeing space enter, how can you say that space arises from the earth?

"If there is no entering or exiting, then space and earth must fundamentally have no different causes; if they are not different, they are identical. If they are identical, then when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?"
This is a refutation by way of reversal.

If you do not see that when earth emerges from the well it enters into space, then the cause (the earth) and the effect (space) would be no different; earth would be identical to space, and space would be identical to earth. When the earth emerges from the well, why do you not see space emerging from the well as well?
"If it is produced by the digging, then the empty space is produced by the digging and should not be considered 'coming forth from the earth';
if it is not produced by the digging, then the digging itself comes forth from the earth—how then can one see the empty space?"
This refutes the arising from the boring tool.

The first three phrases correctly refute the arising from the boring tool: if it is the void that emerges when the tool is used, then the void emerges from the tool itself; how then could one see the earth emerging from the well?
The first three lines do not refute the absence of a cause; rather, the earth emerges because of digging. If there is no cause for the earth, how could there be space?

"Examine this further with precision; examine it closely and observe: the digging proceeds from the human hand and moves according to the direction, while the earth shifts because of the ground. Thus, from what source does this empty space emerge?"
This is a second examination of two points.
Since the earth is excavated and moved out from within the ground, it is said that "the earth has shifted.
A hollow excavation and solid reality cannot function for one another; they are neither a blending nor a conjunction. Therefore, it is illogical that empty space could emerge from nowhere on its own.
This refutes the notion of harmony, as the re-establishment [of the connection] lacks a cause.
"Drilling" and "emptiness" are two distinct entities; "voidness" and "reality" are two distinct meanings. How could these be mutually consistent and thus called "harmony"?
The remaining passages may be understood by themselves.
Third, the reconciliation of the actual meaning has three parts:
first, classifying and connecting with the preceding meanings.

"If this nature of space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unshakable, you should know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are equally called the five great elements; their natures are truly interfused, all being the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction."
The first three phrases reveal the great significance of space.
If space were produced from causes and conditions, its essence would not be all-pervasive and it would be subject to movement; how, then, could it be called "great"?
Now, "Great" (Mahat) signifies being eternal and pervasive. Because it is eternal, it is without birth, extinction, or fluctuation; because it is pervasive, it exists in all times and places.

If it were produced by causes and conditions, it would be present here and absent there, existing now and non-existent later; it would arise when conditions assemble and perish when conditions disperse.
Now, this case is not so; the original *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally all-pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, and is therefore called "Great.
One should know that the following six phrases, by analogy with the preceding four natures, likewise receive the designation "Great."

They are all called "Great" because they are all-pervasive, because they are immovable, because they are the true merits within the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha), and because their great functions, which are without spatial limitation, bring benefit everywhere; how could they be the same as those "expedient means" that have a name but no reality yet are still called "Great"?
2. Rebutting and Exhorting Thorough Investigation: "Ānanda!

Your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate whether empty space is something that comes out, goes in, or neither comes nor goes."
Because it lacks perfect and real wisdom, it is called "darkness"; because it does not comprehend that [the nature] is permanent and pervasive, it is termed "delusion.
If the nature of space were subject to entering and exiting and so forth, its essence would not be permanent, nor would it possess the quality of pervasiveness; how then could it be called "Great"?
Therefore, I urge you to examine this with care.
Third, the correct principle for the present:

"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition."

Ānanda! Just as one empty well is produced from emptiness, so too is the emptiness of the ten directions; it is perfectly pervasive throughout the ten directions—how could it have any specific location?
"Manifesting in accordance with karma.
This can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Fourth, the conclusion rebukes deluded sentiment.

"The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [conditions] as causes and conditions or as arising from spontaneity; all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and devoid of any real meaning."
The nature of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) is likewise so.

In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are frequently mentioned, whereas in the Great Teaching (*Mahāyāna*), the name "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) first appears.

As for the sense-faculties and consciousnesses being designated as "great," this has not yet been seen in the sūtras. In the various perfect and real teachings, one performs a perfect contemplation of all phenomena; the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is all-pervasive and immovable. Although this meaning exists, they do not establish the designation "great."
Now this particular exposition is truly the final and ultimate model for posterity.
The text has four parts:
first, a general indication of the absence of intrinsic nature.
“Ānanda! Seeing and cognition are devoid of intrinsic knowledge; they exist only because of form and space.
2. Extensive refutation by citing examples, in two parts:
First, citing a phenomenon to indicate the underlying principle:

"As you are now in the Jeta Grove, it is bright in the morning and dark at night; even if it were midnight, there would be light during the waxing moon and darkness during the waning moon. Thus, light and darkness are distinguished by means of seeing."
Furthermore, does this vision share the same substance as light and darkness, or with the great empty space?
Is it not of one substance? Or is it both the same and not the same?
"Is it different or not different?
This is an inquiry posed by means of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That is to say, is it one?
Are they different?
Are they both one and different?
Or are they neither one nor different?
2. Refutation by Reasoning: "Ānanda!

If this vision were originally one entity with light, darkness, and space, then the two entities of light and darkness would mutually negate each other; there would be no light when it is dark, and no darkness when it is light."
If it were identical with darkness, then light would cause its disappearance;
if it were necessarily identical with light, then it should be extinguished in the dark. If it were extinguished, how could it see either light or darkness?
"If light and darkness are distinct, yet seeing itself is neither born nor extinguished, how can it be one?
This refutes the notion of oneness.
The first four lines cite the opponent's position; the following four lines establish the principle, while the subsequent six lines provide the logical refutation.
If the seeing were one with its object, then when the object perishes, the seeing would perish; how then could one distinguish between light and darkness?

If the three subsequent lines conclude that this is not the case—since light and darkness are distinct while the seeing does not perish accordingly—one should know that this seeing is not one with its object.

"If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you are separated from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would you discern as the fundamental source of seeing?"

Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from space, this faculty of sight is fundamentally the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; since light, darkness, and space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could sight be established?
This refutes the notion of difference.

The first three phrases cite the opponent's position; the following four phrases constitute the formal refutation, asking what characteristic the object of separation possesses when separated from light; the final four phrases conclude that it ultimately lacks any intrinsic nature.
The preceding sections have all correctly refuted [the opponent's position]; the final three lines below conclude the refutation of light and darkness, which can both be understood as follows:
"Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they be the same?
Apart from these three [elements], they do not exist at all; how could they be different?"
This refutes the notion of "both.

"Identical" means "one"; since light and darkness mutually extinguish one another, they are said to be "opposed. If [the eye] were identical with [light], it would be extinguished along with it, as previously refuted.
Brightness, darkness, and space—apart from these, there is no seeing, nor can it be said to be different from them.
Since the divisions of space and the divisions of seeing originally have no boundaries, how could they not be the same?
Seeing darkness and seeing light—the nature [of the seer] does not change; how then could it not be non-different?
This refutes the "neither-nor" position.
Since empty vision lacks discrimination, it is therefore not "not-one."
Light and darkness shift and pass away one after another, yet in their seeing there is neither birth nor death; therefore, it is not that they are not different.

"Examine this more minutely—examine it with subtle detail, scrutinize it thoroughly, and observe it with clarity: light comes from the sun, darkness follows the dark moon, openness belongs to empty space, and obstruction returns to the great earth. From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise?"
This is a further examination.
I urge you to scrutinize minutely: among the four boundaries, from which does seeing arise?
Seeing and awareness are empty and inert; they are neither a mixture nor a union. Therefore, it is illogical that the essence of seeing should emerge from nowhere on its own.
This refutes the [claim that there is] no cause for the breaking of the harmony.
Third, the reconciliation with the ultimate meaning has three parts:
first, the analogical extension to the preceding meanings.

"If you perceive that the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect and all-pervasive, fundamentally unshakable, you should know that the boundless, unshakable void, along with the shaking elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, are collectively called the six great elements. Their nature is truly and perfectly interfused; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction."
Regarding the statement that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all equally termed "great," this is because they are permanent and pervasive, as explained in the preceding text.
Second, the refutation and exhortation to investigate thoroughly: "Ānanda!..."
Your nature is submerged in delusion; you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should examine this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they born or do they perish?
Are they identical or different?
Are they beyond arising and ceasing?
Are they neither identical nor different?
Arising and ceasing are identical;
non-arising and non-ceasing are distinct.
To regard them as either identical or distinct is to hold both views simultaneously.
Since seeing and hearing are thus authentic, the four propositions cannot be established; it is unmoving yet all-pervasive—is this not the Great One?
Third, the correct assembly of the present principle:

"You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, and the clarity of awareness and the essence of seeing, are pure and fundamental, pervading the Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition."

Just as when the faculty of sight perceives, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; so too with hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, seeing, feeling, and cognition—these wondrous virtues are brilliantly pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids of space. How could they have any fixed location?
"Manifesting according to karma.
"Zeng" (曾) means "formerly" or "previously.

As for "hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching," these refer to the two faculties of nose and tongue; because their objects must come into contact with them before they can be perceived, they are termed "tasting and touching."
The sensation of touch is the body;
the act of perceiving is the mind.
Fourth, the conclusion rebukes deluded sentiments.

"The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature; all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning."
7. The Nature of Consciousness, in four parts:
First, a general statement on its lack of intrinsic nature: "Ānanda!..."
"The nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects.
Second, the extensive refutation by citing examples, which has two parts:
first, citing examples to pose the inquiry.
"Now, survey this assembly of noble ones; let your eyes pass over them one by one. As you look around with your eyes, do so as if in a mirror, without making further distinctions.
Within that [vision], your consciousness should sequentially identify and point out: 'This is Mañjuśrī,' 'This is Pūrṇa,' 'This is Maudgalyāyana,' 'This is Subhūti,' and 'This is Śāriputra.'"
When this consciousness cognizes, does it arise from the seeing,
or from the perceived object, or from space?
"Does it arise suddenly without any cause?
The faculties can illuminate objects, like a mirror reflecting things.
Consciousness can cognize objects, discriminating between self and other.
From what does this discerning consciousness arise?
Second, refuting it through logical reasoning:
"Ānanda!..."

If the nature of your consciousness were born within the faculty of sight, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—the seeing itself would fundamentally not exist;
since the nature of seeing would not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?
This refutes the arising from the sense organs.
If there is form but no seeing, or if there is neither form nor seeing, then since the organ itself has no shape, from what could consciousness arise?

"If your nature of consciousness arises within the object and not from the faculty of seeing, then you would neither see light nor see darkness; if light and darkness are not perceived, then there would be neither form nor emptiness."
"If those marks do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?
This refutes the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
Since mark and vision are mutually dependent, when there is no vision, there are no marks.
"If even the marks do not yet stand, from what could consciousness arise?
If it were born of emptiness, it would be neither mark nor seeing; lacking seeing, there would be no discernment, and one could not know for oneself light, darkness, form, or emptiness.
Without marks, conditions would cease, and seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing would have no place to be established."
The following section refutes the arising of emptiness.
The first two lines establish that [emptiness] does not arise from the sense faculties or their objects.
"It is not seen," and so forth, constitutes the actual refutation; the first three lines refute it by showing that what is not seen cannot distinguish the four objects.
The three phrases beginning with "not characteristics" refute the establishment of the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) through the negation of characteristics.
Characteristics are precisely conditions; since the four objects do not exist, the objective conditions (*ālambana*) are extinguished.
Since the objective conditions do not exist, how can the five sense-faculties exist?
The above points have all been refuted by citing contradictions; they do not rely upon sense organs or objects.
"Abiding in these two negations, emptiness is the same as non-existence;
existence is no different from insentient matter. Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would you distinguish?"
This correctly refutes that consciousness arises from emptiness.
Because it is neither characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor vision (*darśana*), it is called "the non-existence of both," which directly points to emptiness itself.
As for "being equally non-existent," it is because they are ultimately non-existent, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
If one were to say that this emptiness possesses a substantial entity, how could it be like material objects that can be formed or characterized?

Furthermore, this empty space is dark, pure, and devoid of distinction; if this indistinct emptiness were to give rise to anything, that which arises should likewise be indistinct. Therefore, it is said: "What could possibly be distinguished?"
"If it were to emerge suddenly without any cause, why would one not perceive the bright moon during the day?
This refutes the doctrine of causelessness.
Since there is no moon at midday, and consequently no consciousness that perceives the moon, one should know that [consciousness] does not exist without a cause.

“Examine this further with meticulous scrutiny: you see that which relies upon your pupils and projects itself toward external objects; it takes shape as existence and does not take shape as non-existence. From what source, then, does such consciousness arise as its condition?”
"Consciousness moves while vision remains still; they are neither blended nor joined.
This is a further examination of the place of birth.
"Clarity" refers to floating dust, "objects" refer to light and darkness, and "becoming existent or becoming non-existent" refers to empty space.

The two lines following "consciousness moves" conclude that [the senses] are not in conjunction; "movement" refers to the capacity for discernment, while "stillness" refers merely to the illumination of objects.
"Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing" are also like this; consciousness should not arise from nowhere without an object as its condition.
The first two phrases exemplify the refutation of the remaining consciousnesses:
"hearing" and "listening" refer to the ear and nose; "perceiving" and "knowing" refer to the tongue, body, and mental consciousness.
The latter two phrases should not be concluded as "no place of arising," for they concern the conditions by which consciousness arises; thus, they are called "conditions for consciousness."
3. Harmonizing with the True Meaning, in three parts:
1. Analogously extending to the previous meaning:

"If this consciousness-mind originally has no source from which it arises, you should know that its nature—which performs the functions of discerning, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfectly complete, profoundly still, and does not originate from any external object."

Including space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are collectively termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.
The first two phrases constitute the analogy; it should be understood that what follows is the subject of the analogy.

"Discernment" (*vijñapti*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); "seeing and hearing" refers to the sense faculties (*indriya*). Since these are the faculties from which consciousness arises, they are described as "discerning seeing, hearing, and so forth."
2. Rejection and Exhortation to Thorough Investigation: "Ānanda!
Your mind is coarse and flighty; you have not realized that seeing, hearing, clarity, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha."
"You should observe these six sense bases and the consciousness-mind: are they the same or different?
Are they empty or existent?
Are they neither the same nor different, or neither empty nor existent?"
Identity and difference have been refuted in the section on the sense faculties (*indriya*).
"Emptiness" refers to that which arises from emptiness; "existence" refers to the sense faculties and their objects; "neither empty nor existent" refers to the absence of causes.
Third, the correct reconciliation with the present principle.

"You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously aware; this awakened luminosity is the true consciousness. This wondrous awakening is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, encompassing and exhaling the ten voids—how could it have any fixed location?"
"Manifesting according to karma.
Fourth, the conclusion rebukes deluded sentiments:

"The ignorant of the world are confused regarding causes and conditions as well as the nature of spontaneity; all of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discriminating mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever."
III. Realization through the preceding exposition, in two parts:
A. A detailed account of the assembly’s attainment of realization, in two parts:
1. A brief summary of the removal of doubts.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, felt their bodies and minds become vast and empty, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

They realized that the three aggregates and the seven elements are both appearance and nature; they are fundamentally unborn and now, consequently, unceasing. Birth, death, departure, and arrival are all the Tathāgata-garbha—perfectly pervasive and immovable, pure and inherently so. This is the true ultimate nature within the supreme meaning proclaimed by the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "subtle and wondrous instruction."
Because body and mind are perfectly luminous, it is said to be "vast and open.
Since there are no further dharmas that can serve as objects of doubt, there is no obstruction.
Second, the extensive description of the benefits gained, in four parts:
First, the benefit of awakening to the vastness of the mind:

Each member of this great assembly individually realized that their own minds pervade the ten directions, seeing the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing a leaf held in the palm of one's hand.
Previously, one clung to the mind as being within the body, claiming it to be the true nature of the self.
Now one knows that emptiness is within the mind, like a small object held in the palm of the hand.
As the subsequent text also says: "Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean."
2. Understanding all things as truly beneficial.
All things that exist within the entire world are none other than the wondrous, luminous, primordial mind of Bodhi. This essence of mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions.
Previously, one clung to the notion that phenomena exist externally to the mind; now, one awakens to the realization that all phenomena are but mind alone.
Since no phenomenon can be found apart from the true nature (dharmatā), all worldly things are themselves bodhi.
"Bodhi" means awakening; awakening is itself the Buddha. If you maintain that insentient things lack the Buddha-nature, please examine this passage.

Even if one were to believe that insentient things possess the nature, yet still claim they do not possess all dharmas, it would consequently cause the Buddha-nature to be divided into two categories:
first, the Buddha-nature that possesses dharmas, which refers to the nature of sentient beings; [and second, the Buddha-nature that does not possess dharmas].
Second is the nature of Buddha-nature that does not possess the dharma, namely the nature of insentient things.
If this school were to branch out in this way, how would it differ from other teachings that claim insentient grasses and trees lack Buddha-nature?
Now, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows:

"All grasses and trees are the subject (*dharmin*); they necessarily possess all phenomena (*dharmas*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is that they possess Buddha-nature; the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like sentient beings."
The Right Teaching states:

Earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, being the Tathāgatagarbha; this wondrous awakening is profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing and manifesting the ten directions—how could it have any fixed location?
Those who receive this teaching should examine it with full detail.
Third, reflecting upon the benefit of relinquishing the body:

one looks back at the body born of one's parents; it is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions, existing yet as if non-existent, or like a single bubble floating on a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without a trace.

The vast void resides within my mind as easily as a small object held in the palm of my hand; yet when one further contemplates the subtle matter produced therein, how can its size be measured against that of the mind?
Thus, taking a single speck of dust in the air as an example, it is impossible to distinguish whether it exists or perishes, serving as a metaphor for the ultimate minuteness.
The repeated mention of the bubble on the surface of the still water serves as a metaphor for realizing that the body is unborn.

While the previous metaphor still retained a trace of subtle characteristics, the present metaphor shows that characteristics are fundamentally unborn; thus, these two metaphors each clarify a distinct meaning.
Fourth, the benefit of wondrously attaining the primordial mind:
one clearly knows for oneself that one has attained the wondrous fundamental mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable.
"Clearly" (liao) means manifest clarity, as if it were distinct and vivid.
However, "yet" (*rán*) is a particle.
Because clear understanding resides within the mind, it is said that one "knows for oneself.
"Obtains" (*huò*) means to acquire; delusion and falsehood are termed "loss," while awakening and realization are termed "gain."
Since it has already been stated that [the nature] is eternally abiding and indestructible, it is not something newly acquired, but merely made manifest.
Second, Ānanda’s eulogy in verse, which has two parts:
first, the introductory statement.
Prostrating before the Buddha with palms joined, he experienced what he had never known before; thus, in the presence of the Tathāgata, he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.
Having received this benefit within his heart—indeed, having received the Teacher’s instruction—he performed prostrations and extended his praise, recounting how the benefit had inspired his resolve.
2. The actual exposition has four parts:
first, praising the rarity of the Buddha-dharma, which has two sub-parts;
first, the actual praise.
"The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the Śūraṅgama King, rare in the world.
The first phrase praises the Buddha.
The Buddha has three bodies—namely, the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body—and here all are extolled together.

"Wondrously profound" refers to the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body is without marks, profoundly still and eternally quiescent, unconditioned and uncreated, pervading all places because it is neither born nor extinguished.

The *dhāraṇī* is the *saṃbhogakāya*. It refers to that which is manifested through the cultivation of the various *pāramitās* over immeasurable eons; it comprehensively gathers all untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*), sustaining them without loss until the end of the future, remaining indestructible as a recompense for those causes.

The Venerable Acala is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); it refers to the manifestation within the minds of sentient beings—according to their varying capacities and their inclinations toward superior or inferior states—which is the functional aspect of *tathatā* (suchness). This is what is termed a "response."

The Buddha-body is immovable and free from volitional effort; it is like the moon that does not descend nor the hundred waters that do not rise. By the natural power of the roots of goodness of compassion, it is inherently thus. It is also like a reflection appearing according to its form in a mirror, yet the mirror itself remains unmoved; therefore, immovability constitutes the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Furthermore, the characters "wondrous" (miao) and "venerable" (zun) apply both upward and downward; that is to say, the three bodies are of one essence. Though not three, they appear as three. Because their essence, attributes, and functions encompass all meanings, it is called "wondrous";
this is the ultimate consummation.
It is called "Venerable" because it is manifested through ultimate realization.
The second phrase praises the Dharma, which refers here to the Dharma of practice.
This samādhi alone, as revealed by this sutra, is the most venerable and supreme; because it possesses mastery over all dharmas, it is termed a "King."

The first phrase refers to principle and fruit, while the second phrase refers to practice; these three—principle, fruit, and practice—are the meanings to be explained (*vyangya*). Since these meanings can only be manifested through the means of expression (*vyañjaka*), all four dharmas are fully extolled.
2. Exposition of the Benefits:
"It dissolves my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas; without passing through the asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I obtain the Dharma-body.
The first phrase describes the severing of hindrances, which corresponds to the aforementioned state where body and mind are utterly cleared away, resulting in the attainment of non-obstruction.
The subsequent scripture states: "From time immemorial, one has been submerged in and replaced by inversion.
The present mention of "hundreds of millions" is merely a large number used for illustration.

To falsely identify the four elements and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of body and mind, and to mistake oneself for external things—whether perceiving them as vast or minute—all constitute inverted, delusory, and chaotic conceptions.
Now, having heard this instruction, one neither clings to nor recognizes [the mind]; thus it is called "dissolving.
The subsequent phrase, "awakening to the Way," means that one immediately attains the wondrous fundamental mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable.
*Asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable.
*Kalpa* means "period of time.
According to the teachings of the skillful means (*upāya*), all Buddhas cultivate the *pāramitās* throughout innumerable *kalpas* before subsequently attaining Buddhahood.

Now, having attained sudden enlightenment through these words in this assembly, one realizes the wondrous fundamental mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible; how, then, could there be any need to pass through kalpas of *saṃghā*?
Therefore, the following text says: "Resting is itself *bodhi*; it is not obtained from others. Why rely on arduous toil for the sake of cultivation and realization?"
It is also said: "A single snap of the fingers transcends the stage of no-more-learning.
Furthermore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* states: "To know that things are illusory is itself to be free from them; no expedient means need be employed.
To be free from illusion is itself awakening; there is no gradual progression."
All these points convey this same meaning.

However, based on the current text, we shall first describe the stage of intellectual understanding (*jiewu*). As the text says, "Each and every one knows that the mind pervades the ten directions"; here, "knowing" is precisely "understanding. Although this description primarily discusses understanding, it is not devoid of realized awakening (*zhengwu*), for such realization varies according to the depth of the practitioner's entry into the stages.

Furthermore, for instance, those of the two vehicles of the two teachings who have received the provisional [teachings], as well as those of the round teaching whose root-nature has not yet given rise to faith, attain awakening to this realm through understanding;

this is awakening through understanding (*prativedha*). If, however, they have already entered the stages of faith, understanding, and practice, and awaken upon hearing the Dharma, this is awakening through realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Furthermore, for those who have already entered and abide in the stages (*bhūmi*), there is an increase in the Path and a reduction of births.

Up to the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*), the destruction of delusions, the realization of principle, and the manifestation of true, wondrous function are all discussed in terms of their breadth or narrowness according to the depth or shallowness of each respective stage.
Thus, the entire assembly at this single gathering shall all obtain wondrous benefit.
Second, the vow to attain the fruit and deliver sentient beings, which has two parts:
first, the formal presentation of the vow; second, [the explanation of its fulfillment]. First, the formal presentation of the vow:
1. The Expression of the Vow:
“May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.
The first phrase describes wisdom; it is the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
Because one vows to attain realization within this very body, it is said: "I vow now.
The next phrase describes compassion, which is: "I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
The subsequent mention of "eliminating delusions" refers to: "I vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions."
The two dharmas of compassion and wisdom are the bodhicitta, which is precisely the essence of the Path.

Furthermore, by upholding them collectively through essential vows, the three dharmas become fully complete and the four aspirations are perfected; with this, the arousal of the bodhicitta is concluded.
According to the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*, there are three stages of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) in the Sudden Teaching:
first, the realization of the enlightened nature, which is the aforementioned attainment of the wondrous fundamental mind and the realization of the Dharma-body;
second, the arousal of the bodhicitta, which refers to the present two vows of compassion and wisdom.
Regarding the subsequent practice of the bodhisattva path, this refers to the inquiry below concerning the skillful means of cultivation.
It means: if one does not understand one's own mind, how can one know the right path?
Therefore, those who practice for many kalpas are not yet true Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, without first generating the Great Mind (mahācitta), there is no way to initiate practice; thus, Sudhana first declares that he has already generated it before inquiring about cultivation. There is nothing that surpasses this regarding the perfect and sudden cultivation and realization.
2. Statement of Intent:
"To offer this profound mind to every dust-mote world is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

The first phrase aligns with the Buddha’s transformation; through seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below, one realizes, in each instance, the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity through the two minds of compassion and wisdom.
Because it arises from profound principle, it is called the "profound mind.
Because these two minds accord with and follow the transformative practices of the Buddhas throughout the dust-motes of lands—being non-dual and without distinction—it is called "reverent service."

The second line concludes the discussion on repaying kindness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, or offer one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm, if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there would ultimately be no way to repay his kindness."
2. Second, the earnest request for verification:

"I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities; as long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never take parinirvāṇa here."

"My vow to attain enlightenment was originally for the sake of delivering sentient beings; this resolve to deliver them is not a temporary one, but shall last until the end of the future, for only when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted will I enter parinirvāṇa."
This vow is most solemn; therefore, I request you to bear witness to it.
Second, I beg for the removal of delusions so that I may swiftly achieve success:

"O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtlest delusions, enabling me to quickly ascend to Unsurpassed Enlightenment and sit at the site of the Way throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
The first phrase praises his virtues.
He is called "Hero" (*vīra*) because his majestic power is as fierce and magnificent as that of the lion king;
he is called "Powerful" (*bala*) because he is fully endowed with the ten meanings and cannot be subdued.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) means to extract suffering and bestow happiness.
It is called "Great" because it universally rescues all without [discriminating] conditions; this indicates its unsurpassed nature.
The next line requests the removal of delusions.
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in one's own vehicle and the objects of knowledge in the Mahāyāna are both termed "subtle.

Regarding the two subsequent lines that request swift accomplishment: since the preceding text has already expressed the aspiration to attain the fruit, the reason for stating it again here is that, due to the urgency of the mind to deliver sentient beings, there is a wish to attain it early.
The first phrase refers to the True Body (dharmakāya), and the second phrase refers to the manifested response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
"Attaining" (deng) means accomplishment.
"Dharma-hall" (daochang) refers to the manifestation of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
The previous statement that "that which is not yet accomplished does not perish" was discussed in terms of time through a vertical perspective;

the present statement that "[it exists] throughout the worlds of the ten directions" is explained in terms of space through a horizontal perspective, thereby clarifying the aforementioned upward seeking and downward transforming.
Fourth, the metaphor for the immovability of the bodhicitta:
"Though the nature of Śūnyatā may perish, the Śakara-citta does not waver or change.
Śūnyatā means "emptiness."
The nature of empty space cannot be extinguished, yet even that can now be extinguished;
however, the bodhicitta that seeks enlightenment above and transforms beings below never shifts, and is therefore immovable.
*Śakara* means "upright, firm, and indestructible," and it is also translated as "wheel" (*cakra*).

A wheel has the power to crush and grind; this refers to the mind of compassion and wisdom which, in benefiting both oneself and others, is able to crush and grind away afflictions, karma, and suffering.
